EXPUNGEMENT OF OBJECTIONABLE STATEMENTS FROM THE RECORD
speechtext:
On Friday, April 7, the right hon. the leader of the opposition raised the point that the house having control of its own records, the house should, before any statements are expunged from the official report of the debates, pass a resolution to that effect, and he submitted that the Speaker
being the servant of the house in this, as in all matters, the house itself should determine whether anything is to be deleted from any of its records.
In the case in point, the first opportunity I had of fully understanding the words complained of was when I saw the official report, and since I should have ruled them out when they were uttered I consider I was justified in ruling them out from the chair as soon as the house sat again. I agree that in dealing with Hansard the Speaker's authority is subject to the approval of the house.
Instructions for any alteration in the official report of the debates should not be given without communicating them to the house in session, and for this reason, whenever I have deemed it advisable to direct that certain statements be expunged, I have done so from the chair, thus giving a ruling which, under standing order 12, is subject to an appeal to the house. I have followed the precedent established by one of my predecessors who, on April 6, 1925, decided that an answer given by the government should be expunged, and he did so in the following words:
I therefore rule that the answer be expunged from Hansard, and if the question is put again, a distinct answer should be given.
I have dealt with all such cases as questions of order subject to the ordinary rules of parliamentary procedure.

1.	Lease dated December 10, 1907, of the old Beauharnois canal, to William C. McIntyre and Edmond A. Robert (as renewed April 26, 1930) is still in force.
2.	On October 23, 1908, the lease was assigned to the Canadian Light and Power Company, which company now holds renewal of same.
3.	The obligations arising out of the lease are regarded as still in force.
4.	Clauses 16 and 17 of the original lease expressly forbade any assignment of the lease to the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company, its assigns or successors; or any partnership or amalgamation. These clauses were waived by P. C. 3136 of December 18, 1920. This change is not regarded as a change in obligations entailed by the lease.
5.	The reasons set out in the order in council waiving clauses 16 and 17 were to the effect that the provisions of the clauses in question caused the company great hardship in financing its operations and prevented it from borrowing at advantageous rates on its securities, and had hampered the company's development, tending to increase the cost of power to the public.
6.	Not specifically, but it is provided therein that there shall be no assignment except with the approval of the governor in council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:

The holders of the $30,000,000 6 per cent collateral trust bonds of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company held a meeting called in accordance with the provisions of the trust mortgage deed securing the said bonds, default having been made in the payment of the interest thereon, and elected a committee to deal with the situation. In the event of any plan being submitted, it would be for the committee to consider what appropriate action should be taken, but the committee would undoubtedly ascertain the views of the government with respect to its guarantee. The committee of the bond holders is charged with the responsibility of dealing with the plans for reorganization of the enterprise, and not the government.

Mr. ISAAC D. MACDOUGALL (Inverness): Mr. Speaker, before offering any comment on the budget or the criticism to which it has been subjected may I pause briefly to pay a humble meed of tribute and of praise to the memory of a personal friend, a fellow commoner from the maritime provinces who, since the beginning of this session, has passed on to that bourne from whence no traveller returns. The late Mr. Cormier, who all too briefly represented in this house the constituency of Restigouche-Madawaska, was in every sense of the word an educated, cultured, Christian gentleman. He exemplified in
private as in public life the highest and noblest traditions of the French Acadian race in Canada, a race whose unselfish sacrifices, indomitable courage and fortitude in the face of travail and adversity; whose respect for law and constituted authority, whose love of home, and abiding faith in a triune and eternal God combined to earn for it a distinctive place in the annals of maritime history. To that race, which through the passing of Mr. Cormier has lost a distinguished representative; to the electorate of Restigouche-Madawaska ; to the many friends of the deceased and especially to his immediate relatives, on this occasion I extend my sincer-est condolences.
Mr. Speaker, as a fellow Nova Scotian may I be permitted-if he can stand any more felicitations-to felicitate my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) on the presentation of his second budget to the parliament of Canada. My hon. friend-and I wish he would not look at me at the moment, because I know 'his native modesty-has earned for himself an exalted place in Canadian public life. For some years he occupied the position which you, siir-and may I congratulate you also on having reached to-day the sixtieth anniversaa'y of your birth-occupy at the moment with such ability, impartiality and urbanity, the position of chief commoner of Canada. On two oooasions my hon. friend was selected by his fellow citizens of Nova Scotia to be premier of that province. When my hon. friend accepted the portfolio of finance he brought to the discharge of onerous public duties a keen sense of business acumen, a wide knowledge of men and affairs, natural intellectual endowments that are not surpassed in the House of Commons, 'high educational qualifications, and perhaps above all and more important than anything else an unsullied and irreproachable character. During the world depression and dislocation of to-day I think we can all agree, irrespective of party politics, that Canada is most fortunate in having the present Minister of Finance.
But let me have done with congratulations for the moment, Mr. Speaker; that is hardly a Highlander's role. I turn now to the speech of my hon. friend who so ably represents Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), oveT the long distance telephone from Montreal. From the point of view of time my hon. friend's speech was the longest he has made in parliament; from the point of view of delivery it was the loudest, -and from the point of view of material it was by far the emptiest of his public addresses. From its exordium to the colourless and broken-backed amend-
The Budget-Mr. Macdougall

menit with which it concluded there was not even the genesis of one constructive idea. But perhaps no one who has been in this house for the last few years would be surprised at that. For several years pa&t the sole role of our friends opposite has been to offer carping, destructive criticism. It would be just as futile, just as bootless, to expect anything of a constructive nature to emanate from the opposition benches as it would be to put a blind man in a dark room and expect him to discover a black cat that was not there.
My hon. friend, in the beginning of his speech, essayed the role of prophet, a role that sits rather heavily upon him, because as I understand in the last election he made some predictions that proved entirely unwarranted. In this role he predicted that there would be changes in the budget before it passed its final stages in parliament. May I tell him that there never was a budget presented to the parliament of Canada, either by a Liberal or by a Conservative government, in which material changes were not made before it passed'its final stages. But, sir, it does not lie in the mouth of any Liberal to talk about changes being made in the budget after its introduction. We all remember what happened in 1927. When the Liberal government of that day brought down its budget, one of the features of that budget was a reduction in the duty on automobiles. Shortly after the budget was presented to parliament a very large delegation of working men and also women engaged in the automobile manufacturing industry of Canada, stormed the citadel hill. The government of that day declared that they would stick to their guns, that nothing would be done to satisfy the automobile manufacturers. They paid no attention to that delegation of workmen, nor to other delegations that came to them. But when the automobible manufacturers themselves interviewed them, what happened? In the dead and darkness of the night-it must have been in the night because nothing was done that day-in the darkness of the night, I say, when evil deeds are wont to be perpetrated, my hon. friends sought and found a method of relief for the automobile manufacturers of Canada, and to the amazement of this country the very next day they reduced the sales tax on automobiles and completely wiped out the luxury tax, with the result that they put the manufacturers of automobiles in a more preferred position than they had been in before the Liberal party tinkered with the tariff at all. And if Dame Rumour be a wench of her word, as she sometimes is, in grateful

acknowledgment a couple of years later of this sneaking, contemptible, subterranean and typical Grit method of escape that was given to the automobile manufacturers of Canada by the then Liberal government, these same manufacturers pledged large sums to the campaign fund of the Liberal party in 1930.
I say therefore to my hon. friend from Shelbume-Yarmouth that it lies not in the mouth of any Liberal to talk about changes being made in the budget before it reaches its final stages in parliament. After assuming the role of prophet, my hon. friend went on to take the role of financial critic, and he criticized the government of the day because in its financial presentation it dealt with net debt and not with funded debt, forgetting, with that blissful forgetfulness of the Liberal party, that for nine years budgets were presented by the Liberal government and dealt solely and entirely with the net debt and not with the funded debt. The hon. gentleman also criticized the Minister of Finance for not laying aside a sinking fund. That is something that is becoming quite important to the Liberal party. In the days of buoyant revenues, before the world became enthralled in the present depression and when there was an opportunity to set aside a sinking fund, my hon. friends were in power for nine years and took no steps to set aside such a fund. But with that inconsistency which is the dominant characteristic of the Liberal party, the hon. gentleman censures the Minister of Finance for not setting aside a sinking fund in this period of depression.
The hon. member also referred to the fact that there were increases in the national debt, and it is true that there have been increases. But is there any man in Canada, who is not a fit and proper candidate for a lunatic asylum, who would think that there would be no increases in the national debt? This country, in common with every other country, had to meet an extraordinary situation and make extraordinary expenditures, and I do not hesitate to say that the increase in the national debt was justified. Those who argue otherwise must take the responsibility for saying that this government should refuse to discharge the fundamental right of a government in regard to the unemployed; they must say that the government should not have come to the rescue of those farmers in Saskatchewan who were suffering on account of circumstances over which they have no control. Extraordinary expenditures with respect to all these matters resulted in an increase in the national debt, but in every instance the increase was absolutely necessary.

The Budget-Mr. Macdougall
And this is true of every government that recognizes the functions and the duties of government. They could not have been avoided.
My 'hon. friend next dealt with the stabilization fund proposed in the budget. This he damned with faint praise. He spoke mostly in reference to the maritime provinces in dealing with this matter, but he forgets that the farmers in the maritimes are still producing pork, poultry and cattle, even though he has left, and this stabilization fund will be of great benefit to them. He dealt with the stabilization fund only as it applied to fish; and of course, in the political blindness of prejudice 'that obscured his otherwise clear vision, he said, "Why this refers to only $50,000 worth of fish." My hon. friend must surely know, as I believe he does, that the fish products of the Atlantic and Pacific coast affected by the stabilization fund, did not amount to $50,000 but over three million.

When I listened to my hon. friend making his statement I was not at all surprised that he was only about sixty-five per cent unfair to the present government. What I did wonder at is that he could be thirty per cenit fair to them. Knowing the deep dyed partisanship of my hon. friend, I could almost visualize the political labour pains he must have suffered in making a statement that was even thirty per cent fair to the present government in a matter redounding to its credit.
My hon. friend says that the right thing to do is to cancel the licences of the beam trawlers. For the purpose of being fair to him, let me go into the history of beam trawler operations in Nova Scotia. The first permit ever granted to a fish corporation to operate beam trawlers was granted by a Liberal government. To come nearer to the present time and to the time when my hon. friend joined the government in 1922, permits expired for the operation of beam trawlers in Nova Scotia and they were renewed by the King government for the benefit of the fish corporations. The permits expired again in 1923 and again they were renewed by the King government for the benefit of the fish corporations. The same thing happened in 1924 and 1925, but in 1926 my hon. friend, the present official critic of the opposition and the champion of the shore fishermen of Nova Scotia, entered this house as a member of the King government. The fishermen surely had a right to believe my hon. friend would make some protest against the renewal of permits, but the months wore on and the time came around in 1926 to renew the permits for beam trawlers. They were again renewed and the permits this time bore not only the imprimatur of the Prime Minister of that day but the nihil obstat of my hon. friend the member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, And to use his own words, women wept and the fishermen bowed their heads.
In 1927, 1928 and 1929, we had the same procedure, but in 1930, with a federal election on and after a report of a commission appointed to investigate the fisheries in the maritime provinces, steps were taken by order in council. I am sorry the leader of the

But in 1930, what was done? A tax was levied by order in council on beam trawler caught fish. When my hon. friends levied that tax by order in council, and unconstitutionally, if I may use the term of my hon. friend in regard to matters of taxation, because they did not consult parliament, they knew the order in council would be annulled by the courts of the country. As a matter of fact, to my knowledge defeated Liberal candidates went to fish corporations in Nova Scotia and said: "Never mind, do not worry about this tax; it is only a little Grit stageplay; it will never be collected." I am unalterably opposed to their operation, and I shall continue to support the fishermen of Nova Scotia who, through their cooperative unions, desire that beam trawlers shall not be allowed to operate in the fisheries of Nova Scotia. I congratulate the government on going as far as they did, and while they did not go as far as I would like to see them go, and I say that frankly, I trust that next year when additional representations are made, they will go a great deal further in this matter.
Here may I pay a tribute to the personal representative of Premier Harrington who so strongly urged upon the government not merely that the number of licences granted to beam trawlers should be reduced, but that they should not be allowed to operate at all in the province of Nova Scotia so far as the power of this government could prevent it. Those of us who believe that the beam trawler is furnishing competition which is unfair to the shore fishermen are prepared to carry the fight on until the beam trawler method of fishing is entirely suppressed, because in my judgment and in that of a great many more, in the judgment I believe of ten out of eleven fishermen in the province of Nova Scotia, it is a destructive method of prosecuting the fisheries.
Another matter was placed on the order paper which is of vital importance to the fishermen of the maritime provinces, and that was the resolution standing in the name of my good friend from Antigonish-Guysborough in reference to reciprocity. May I congratulate him upon placing that resolution on the order paper? He was fearless in his attitude towards reciprocity, but I noticed that he did not get very much support for his resolution from the Liberal party.

speechtext: We have not had a chance yet.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The resolution was
adopted by the government. My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), though he is a very tall man, is always able to succeed in pulling himself up in sections to discuss almost any matter. I have seen no lack of jumping to his feet to discuss other matters. I have had many requests from Liberals in my constituency for the speech delivered on that occasion by the right hon. leader of the opposition on the subject of reciprocity, and I was very much pained to have to say in complying with those requests that it was the shortest speech that I had ever heard the right hon. gentleman make, because he said nothing.
Perhaps there is some little difficulty between the machine that controls the Liberal party in Halifax and my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough, but I do not see why he should not have had support from his own party in this house for his resolution. Furthermore, the same resolution was introduced by a Liberal in the city of Halifax when nominating a Liberal candidate for the provincial house. I presume that he was a friend of my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough, and he was made to withdraw his resolution.
In regard to reciprocity, I have always believed in a reciprocity treaty between Canada and the United States, but I make this statement, and there is not a man in public life who can deny it, that there never was any intention in 1911 on the part of the government of Canada of that day, or on the part of the United States, to enter into a reciprocity treaty. I do not hear that denied by any hon. member. If they attempted to deny it, I would quote the words of the Right Hon. W. S. Fielding who, speaking in this house in 1922, said that what was proposed:
-was not a treaty but a comprehensive agreement which was entered into in 1910-11 as the house will remember.
It was not a treaty.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a fine distinction.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am just going to
point out to my hon. friend, who may not be able to catch fine distinctions, what the fine distinction is. A comprehensive trade agreement can be cancelled overnight without notice being given by either of the contracting parties, but a treaty cannot be cancelled. It is for some specified time. Surely that, is not too fine a distinction for my hon. friend to catch.
I want to make this statement, although it may not find favour with hon. gentlemen opposite, that we are nearer to-day to a
The Budget-Mr. Macdougall

reciprocal trade treaty with the United States than we have been since 1911. Why was it that hon. gentlemen opposite who were in office in this country until 1930, and were so loud in their advocacy of reciprocity, never sought reciprocal trade arrangements with the United States. Time and time again on the floor of this house the leader of the party opposite was challenged in that regard, and he never committed himself as to whether he would ever seek, or whether he even desired, reciprocal trade arrangements with the United States-never.
And why is it that we could not have made a reciprocal trade treaty with the United States during the last ten years? The answer will be found in the trade returns of this country. Why should the American government enter into reciprocal trade arrangements with us when, under the weak-kneed trade policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, we had handed over to the Americans almost everything they wanted from the Canadian market without asking from them anything in return? Let me quote a few' figures for my hon. friend. In 1928, for example, under this wise fiscal policy of my hon. friends opposite, Canada imported from the United States 8825,651,549 worth of goods, and in 1929, the year before hon. gentlemen opposite went to the country and when they had not yet felt the full force of Beauharnois, we imported 8893,585,482 worth of American goods. We exported to the United States in 1928, 8491,566,297 worth of goods, and in 1929, $522,677,767. Do you think that the United States would ever seek a reciprocal trade treaty with us when they had a favourable trade balance to thia/t extent which was granted to them by the unwise fiscal policy of the previous administration? But to-day we have a party in power which has placed restrictions upon the flood of American goods entering Canada. To-day we have something to bargain with. That is the answ'er. As a result we are nearer to a reciprocal trade treaty with the United States than we have ever been in the last thirty years. But when that trade treaty is made-
I do not know about my hon. friends opposite, but I suppose that following their glorious record of inconsistency, they may hot support it-we on this side of the house, if that trade treaty does eventuate, have full confidence that the right hon. the Prime Minister will see that the position of Canada be safeguarded and that the treaty, if it is signed, will be mutually advantageous to Canada and the United States.

The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth had something to say concerning the coal industry of the province of Nova Scotia, and in his remarks twitted the Minister of Mines (Mr. Gordon), suggesting that the government had not done all it should have done for that industry. In case there may be illusions in the minds of the people of Nova Scotia in connection with this matter, I shall spread on the records of Hansard exactly what the government has done for the coal industry and the people in the native province of my hon. friend and myself. Before giving the figures, I challenge the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, or any other hon. member, to dispute the statement that the Bennett government has done more for the coal mining industry of Nova Scotia than has any government we have had in Canada.

I ask the hon. member
simply to look at the coal industry in Nova Scotia to-day.

I make the statement that the present government has done more for the Nova Scotia coal industry than has any government which has held power since the Canadian union was consummated. I am not at all criticizing hon. members opposite for the little they did to assist the coal industry when they were in power. They made a step in the right direction, but that step was not sufficiently long.
Under order in council P.C. 539, of 1928- and I say to the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, quite frankly, that he had something to do with the passage of it-114,010 tons of coal were shipped from Nova Scotia under the assisted rates; the cost to the government of that day was $65,760, and the cost per ton for movement of the coal was 57-6 cents. In 1929, still under the administration of hon. members opposite, the tonnage of coal shipped from Nova Scotia under P.C. 539 was 304,744, the cost was $206,019.98 and the cost per ton 67-6 cents. Although during part of the year 1930 order in council No. 1300 applied, the tonnage from Nova Scotia under the assisted rates amounted to 371,800 tons, the cost was $214,142.58, and the cost per ton 57-7 cents. In 1931, under orders in council 539 and 1300, the tonnage shipped from Nova Scotia mines under the assisted rates was 403,976 tons, the cost to the government of Canada was $228,625.62, and the

The Budget-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
average cost per ton was 56-6 cents. In 1932, under the assisted rates granted by this government, the Nova Scotia coal operators shipped into central Canada 711,589 tons, the cost to the government of Canada was $538,110.16, and the average cost per ton was 75-6 cents.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget covers a wide field, involving many important changes. Having regard to the basic tariff and financial policies of the government, as indicated by their action since 1930, I certainly favour a number of these changes. I am prepared of course to support the tariff reductions, the income tax proposals, the wheat marketing assistance, and agricultural stabilization.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) had something to say regarding the government's assistance to wheat marketing, and wound up with words to the effect that instead of gambling in wheat the government should take its loss, get out and be rid of the transaction. I do not believe the western farmers want the government to get out.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member should read the whole passage.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon.
members must realize that there is a difference between what is known as gambling and assistance to provide a market.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I say,
however, that if a farmer sells his wheat in the fall and buys options he may be accused of gambling, but in so doing he would be doing exactly the same thing as if he kept his wheat in a granary all winter, awaiting a favourable opportunity to haul it out. In effect he would be running exactly the same risk. For those reasons I believe the criticism is not well taken. Time will show, when the final figures are given to the house, to what extent the government is involved and to what extent it may lose money. But I do not believe it would be fair to say that, if the government loses some money in connection with the stabilization of the wheat market, it should be condemned. Undoubtedly the stabilization of the wheat market is of vastly greater importance to the three western provinces than
it is to the rest of 'Canada. However in ascertaining whether or not a certain policy is fair to the whole country one must consider all factors, one must balance all the policies of the government, and their advantages or disadvantages to every part of Canada.
There can be no doubt that tariff legislation is of more advantage to Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia than to the three prairie provinces. It is possible that when the maritime provinces advanced their claims for additional moneys and bonuses by way of freight rates, the western provinces may have felt that the maritimes had received special consideration. It is possible that the maritimes may feel that in connection with wheat stabilization the west is receiving special consideration. I say, however, that if we are going to be fair to every part of Canada we must consider not one policy, but the combination of all policies, and do our best to weigh their advantages and disadvantages. The business of the government and parliament is to see that so far as possible the advantages and disadvantages balance so that the various parts of Canada may share equally. I believe I would be stating the opinion of the maritimes as truly as the hon. member stated the opinions of western farmers if I were to say that the government should pull out and take its loss, so far as the maritimes are concerned. Were I to take that stand I would be as near the truth as was the hon. member when he said that the western farmers want the government to pull out of the wheat market altogether. Certainly that is not so, as far as the farmers in my constituency are concerned. I believe the stabilization fund will be of some advantage. There is no question that it was the loss due to exchange that put the cooperative pool practically out of the business of shipping cattle to the old country. Even if it were one hundred per cent true that the cost of paying this amount to those who undertake to export cattle, getting rid of the five per cent surplus, must be borne by the ninety-five per cent of the cattle sold in Canada, it would in my judgment still be a substantial advantage to the farmers of Canada. For it is a hopeless task to try to market ten head where are are only purchasers for nine. Whether or not some day, under conditions where supply and demand are just about equal, we will be able to work out something better in price control, this is the only thing possible to-day.

The Budget

Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
I want to reier in passing to the question of the royal commission on banking. The Macmillan committee in the old land found its terms of reference, which appear to be fairly wide, were still not wide enough to enable them to deal with the issues they thought it necessary to deal with. I want to call attention to a few words in the concluding note of the full committee:
We have now completed all the recommendations which we are able to make for remedial action by the monetary machine itself. If our recommendations relating to international action are given effect, we should hope for a great improvement in the situation in due course. If, however, progress along these lines is delayed or if the action taken is insufficient, we believe that our own monetary authorities will not be able to remedy matters without assistance from changes in other non-monetary factors by which the volume of our domestic output and employment, and in particular our balance of trade, are also much influenced.
Several members of the committee made additional recommendations. I say that as a result of that experience we should see that the terms of reference to the banking commission do not confine the commission to inquiring into banking alone, but if certain changes in monetary policy are found desirable then the commission should have reasonable power to enable them to deal with these other matters as well, as far as they are directly connected with changes they may recommend in monetary policy.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I agree with a good deal that has been said about the budget. I have already stated that I am supporting certain matters initiated, and certain policies embodied in the budget. But it is a deflationist budget. That is made quite clear by certain words of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) and on that ground we challenge it. It is said that Naaman the Syrian, captain of the hosts of the king of Syria was a great man with his master and honourable. He was also a mighty man in valour but he was a leper. The budget is a comprehensive review of Canada's financial situation, it proposes many changes of importance, some of them good and some not so good, but it is a deflationist budget. I do not agree with those who say that in Canada we are bound up altogether with world conditions and that we can do nothing by ourselves. I cannot agree that the policies of the government alone are entirely to blame for the present price levels and the present situation in Canada. But it is taking a hopeless position to say that because of world conditions we. can do nothing. It is just as foolish as to say that everything that has happened in Canada in the 
way of distress and unemployment is due to the policy of this government or any other government. We must consider what we can do on our own part with regard to money, with regard to tariffs, as well as what we can do in cooperation with others. And the test to be applied to any government is whether, of itself as a national government, it has taken action along the lines it should, and whether in addition to that it has offered cooperation along the lines best calculated to improve the world situation and the national situation as well.
I have said that the budget is based on deflation. This is clearly shown by the words of the Minister of Finance as reported at page 3208 of Hansard:
During the past year Canada was the only foreign country that was able to borrow in the public markets of the United States.
This enviable position has been and can be held only by the maintenance of sound financial and monetary policies. Much has been heard in recent months about inflation. Some of the advantages claimed for inflation may seem alluring to industries harassed by falling prices and declining turnover. But let the sponsors of inflation never forget that apart from the other difficulties and dangers involved in their program, one inevitable result would be a flight from our dollar, a withdrawal on a large scale of the capital invested by foreigners in this country in the form of securities and bank deposits. There are also to be considered internal reactions to any steps which might impair confidence in a country's currency. Against policies which might lead to such dangers, this government has resolutely set its face.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think it can be said, if that defines the government's position correctly, that the government says we will have no inflation. They stand, for the present at least, by the deflation of recent years, which in three years since 1929, in credit and currency amounts to approximately $700,000,000. We have challenged that policy by an amendment, calling for controlled inflation. Those who stand by the gold basis, as far as it has been possible to stand by it-but I do not think we can take that position very seriously, since so many nations have abandoned the gold basis

but those who stand by it in theory seem to think it is a limitation on the amount of currency that may be. issued, and so prevents uncontrolled inflation. I do not think, however, that inflation and deflation are necessarily tied up with or free from the gold basis at all. I think you can have both on the gold basis, if any country to-day is on the gold basis. What is inflation and deflation? The best definition that I have come across is given by Doctor Marvin, the econo-

The Budget-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
mist of the Royal Bank. In a few sentences he gives us inflation, deflation and stabilization. This was an address delivered, I think, in Montreal about two years ago:
When credit was expanding at the same rate as production, the price level remained steady. It is true that the price level depends upon the ratio of credit and production. When credit expands excessively, prices rise, and when credit is unduly contracted, prices fall. When the volume of credit is kept proportionate to the volume of production, prices remain stable. These last three sentences constitute the whole story of what was wrong with the engine and tell how distribution can again be made to function.
Irving Fisher, in chapter III of his book on The Money Illusion, answers the question, Why does money fluctuate? He says:
The question now arises, Why does money thus change in its buying power? The answer, in brief, is "relative inflation and deflation." The emphasized word "relative" means inflation or deflation relative to the volume of trade in any given period.
There are two or three things that enter into the question of the variation in the purchasing power of money. When we say money we mean the money that circulates, whether based on bank credit, figures in bank books, actual currency, silver and copper coins; it is all money, all buying power. Inflation, then, is simply an increase in the volume of money, and the velocity of circulation as well, relative to the amount of goods and the state of trade in the country. Deflation is simply the opposite, and it is because we have had so much deflation since 1929 that we are calling for a controlled inflation at least back to the place we he'd, so far as credit was concerned, in 1929. For the moment I am not arguing that this was the only factor that helped break prices. It has been said that we have everything in Canada now that we had in 1929 except the flow of money, but that is not right. We have not the demand for wheat that existed before 1929, but simply because the world demand for wheat fell off I do not see that we should superimpose on the industrial structure of this country a ruinous policy of deflation, and thus intensify the depression. If our farmers were to take that position and stop raising the amount of wheat they have been raising what would happen? If our railways were allowed to cut off services what would happen? If our medical men cut down the service they give simply because they are not getting the returns they received previous to 1929 what would happen to the health of our people? If the lawyers took the same position what would be the result? Why should we not look for something in the nature of stabilization, when so many economists tell us that the volume of money in circulation determines what will be the price level? This is an important factor, though it does not determine it absolutely. Instead of a policy of deflation I think we should have had an attempt on the part of the banks to keep money in circulation.
What are the arguments against reasonable inflation? The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) stated in Toronto some time ago that those who were supporting inflation were calling for something like what happened in Germany during and after the war. There is no doubt that there are dangers in connection with inflation, but there are other and perhaps greater dangers in connection with deflation. We cannot get away from danger; we must try to adopt a reasonable course. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance, in his speech in London last December, pointed out that Canada should not depart from the position of sound money; he said that if our dollar were on a parity with the pound sterling for twelve months it would cost Canada approximately $150,000,000. The hon. gentleman was supported in that statement by Sir Thomas White, and a few days ago in Winnipeg we' had the statement by Mr. Jackson Dodds, manager of the Bank of Montreal. He held up some stamps that were taken off letters which came from Germany in 1923, at the height of inflation; he said we might expect to pay a good many dollars to send a letter around the country if we adopted a policy of inflation.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that it is utterly ridiculous to argue that because Germany inflated in that way we should not reflate or inflate back to where we stood in this country in 1929 with regard to the volume of credit, without running the same risk. If we did that and we had the same fall in the dollar that took place in the mark in Germany, wheat would be worth $716 a bushel.

speechtext:
It would not take long to
pay off the mortgage.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
John
Maynard Keynes, in his book Monetary Reform, states that Germany's pre-war currency totalled six milliard gold marks, an average of about $25 per head. In 1920 it totalled eighty-one milliards, and by August of 1923 it had increased to 116 thousand milliards. Is it fair to say that because Germany did that in the years 1920 to 1923 we would do the same thing in Canada? Every nation inflated during the war; Canada, the United States and Great Britain, yet nearly every nation was back on the gold
3874	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
standard by 1925. They did not allow it to go uncontrolled. What was the position of Germany? She started her inflation in earnest after she was defeated. I refer again to John Maynard Keynes, in his book, The Economic Consequences of the Peace:	All
her fleet was ceded to the allies, together with her overseas possessions and property. The allies reserved the right to retain and liquidate all property rights and interests belonging to and controlled by German nationals within the former German colonies. In Alsace-Lorraine the same provisions applied; the allies reserved the right to retain and liquidate all property rights and interests belonging to German nationals in their territory. Article 260 of the financial clauses provided that the reparation commission might demand within one year the expropriation of German nationals and the delivery to the commission of any right and interest of German nationals in any public utility in China, Turkey, Austria, Hungary and Bulgaria. Germany renounced her right to any participation in any financial or economic organization of an international character operating in any of the allied or associated states, in Austria, Hungary, Bulgaria, Turkey or any dependencies of those states, or in the former Russian empire. One-way tariffs were established between Germany and Alsace-Lorraine. Upper Silesia, with a plebiscite ceded to Poland 22 per cent of the German output of hard coal, and the Saar mines were ceded to France. It has been said that Germany was built on blood and iron. That is not so; Germany was built on coal and iron. The Rhine, Upper Silesia and the Saar made possible her steel, chemical and electrical industries. The total reparation bill was $40,000,000,000, and under these impossible terms she inflated and absolutely wiped out all her internal debt. She was the same credit risk after the war that a man would be who had been convicted of some heinous criminal offence and against whom a judgment had been issued for three or four times what he was worth, with practically all his civil rights taken from him. Would anyone say that Canada today could be compared to Germany at that time? That will not go; some better argument than that will have to be brought forward. We have inflated under the stress of war and other national circumstances, and we did not let it get out of hand. There is no reason in the world why we should not do what we can to raise the price level, through our monetary policy, by a reasonable inflation in Canada, though I do not say that this would cure all our troubles at once.

The next point, of course, is to what point we should inflate. When would you come to the point where you would stop inflation and, if possible, attempt to control any further increase in prices? I think Sir Josiah Stamp said that point would be somewhere around the average of 1924 to 1928. In any case it must be a place which will establish a reasonable parity between the earning power of the people, the expenses of government and the debts of the country, private, municipal, provincial and federal. What was wrong with the conditions existing in this country between 1924 and 1928? We were able to balance government budgets, no matter whether those governments were Liberal, Conservative or Farmer; we were able to advance reasonable public works, railways and municipal improvements, and I do not believe the creditor class suffered particularly because of the fact that the purchasing power of money was not what it is to-day. I do not think there is any question of the fact that during that period we had a reasonable parity between the general price level and our debts, the cost of government and so on. I submit therefore that that would be a reasonable point to aim at. I do not know whether experience will show that we can get there; we cannot get there so far as wheat is concerned. I am certain, however, that even if we cannot get there with regard to wheat, this country dare not liquidate on the basis of the present level of Wheat prices. The statesmen of Great Britain as well as of Canada have recognized that. We know that to bring other commodities down to the level of wheat prices, to bring wages down, would mean absolute ruin to the country. In Winnipeg the other day Jackson Dodds said that we should have to do that, among other things. He said:
"Before better times can come," he added, "competition in depreciation of currencies must cease; international debts must be adjusted, tariff barriers which have been erected beyond peace time needs must be lowered reciprocally, permitting of exchanges of goods, and payments in goods; government expenditures and taxes must be decreased; budgets must be balanced -which in our own case include federal, provincial and municipal-wages and prices must be brought into proper relationship again, so that prices received by farmers and other producers of raw materials may be brought into balance with prices of products of the factory, thus restoring activity and employment in cities and so increasing the demand for the products of the farm and factory, providing traffic for railways and ships. . .
Such a policy would greatly increase our debts.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hear, hear.

The Budget-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon.
friend says "hear, hear." Well, the significant part of the debt of the country is not what the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth pointed out, that there has been added to the national debt within the last three years or so about 8400,000,000. What is of significance is that all debts have been doubled-not the $400,000,000, but all debts-because of a drop in commodity prices; and if we must drag down labour, if we must drag down factory prices to the level of wheat prices as they are to-day, then we are also going to drag the creditors down without any question. It means therefore wholesale liquidation, and we cannot do it without increasing our debts in the first place. It is possible that if nothing can be done to increase the prices of primary products we shall be forced to do that, but it will mean a tremendous sacrifice and terrible hardships so far as the Canadian people are concerned.
The Prime Minister himself indicated this pretty well at the Imperial conference. I quote from Annex III, statement made before the committee on monetary and financial questions by the Prime Minister of Canada, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett:
Canada, like all other countries, has suffered severely from the calamitous fall in commodity prices. Since August, 1929, our index of wholesale prices has fallen 32 per cent and is now only 4 per cent above the pre-war level. This means that the dollar has increased in purchasing power by 48 per cent. As a result of this rapid and persistent decline in the general price level and the inevitable disparities created between different kinds of prices, normal business relationships have been disrupted, profit margins have disapeared in many cases, enterprise has been discouraged, unemployment has steadily increased, the fiscal problems of all our public bodies have been greatly aggravated, and the burden of fixed charges is exerting an almost intolerable pressure upon some of the strategic elements in our national economy. . . . Interest charges represent the most important of the fixed or semi-rigid element in our cost structure. If prices remain on their present level, such charges will constitute an intolerable or almost intolerable burden in many cases. Even if it can be borne, the fortuitous gain to the creditor of 40 to 48 per cent in general purchasing power above what he contracted for appears to be a grave injustice.
I agree with that, but judging by some statements that have been made subsequently, I take it that the government has not thoroughly grasped the gravity of the injustice. There is one statement made by Jackson Dodds with which I heartily agree, because it is a satisfactory statement.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Only one.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just one.
He says:
"It is an elementary fact," he remarked, "that one must return whatever one borrows- whether it be a book, a lawn-mower, a guinea or an American dollar. No abstruse question of exchange enters into it so far as the lender is concerned: he merely wants back what he lent, plus the hire of interest according to agreement. Certainly we in Canada would not have accepted at par German marks. . .
Now that is exactly what we want, and it is because we believe that deflation in Canada has made it impossible to pay back the kind of dollars we borrowed that we want inflation. We do not borrow dollars to eat; we borrow dollars to buy food, clothing, lumber and so on, and other necessaries of life. A reasonably honest dollar, a sound dollar, is one which you can borrow at the beginning of the year and repay at the end of the year, being sure that its purchasing power will remain the same or reasonably the same; and it is because the present dollar does not do this that we are opposed to it.
What is sound money? I have been trying, in all the speeches I have read and in the various declarations that have been made in this house, to find out what sound money is. It is not the kind of money we have in Canada to-day, because the Prime Minister himself said that the present situation was a grave injustice to those who had borrowed money; and you cannot have a sound monetary policy nor sound social conditions based on a grave injustice. The only sound dollar is the dollar that is within reason stable in its purchasing power from year to year. We believe that at least a reasonable inflation will tend partly to bring that about-it will not do it alone, but it will tend to do it in part- and that is why we are asking for reasonable reflation or inflation.
Sound money is just a catchword. I remember I used to argue years ago with a socialist friend of mine in Alberta about socialism, and when I began to ask him questions he could not answer, he always ended up by saying, "It's the hell of a system we are living under." I could not answer that; it was not an argument.

speechtext: It was a description.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We find another catchword in the Acts of the Apostles. The silversmiths met together when they found that Paul was telling the people that the silver images they were making were not gods, and Demetrius got his followers together and said, "You had better come with me and we will protest against this heresy of Paul's. We are

ask, Mr. Speaker, if the problem was not manfully 'tackled and skilfully handled. There are those who complain to-day that the government has not healed this running sore. There are those who criticize the government because millions are still required each year by 'the government railways, but may I ask: What is it possible to do? Who has suggested any possible remedy which would enable the government to escape from the liability of its endorsement of the Canadian National bonds? Has the Canadian Pacific Railway ever offered to assume the liabilities of the Canadian National? Let us merge these railways; let us give them away; let us wash them into the sea, but the burden of $60,000,000 to $70,000,000 of interest due each year will remain. I have given no small amount of thought and no small amount of honest endeavour to the study of the problem. I fail to see how any action that the government might have taken in the last three years at the dictation or invitation of the most wise could have delivered this country from the burden which weighs upon it to-day. Ft is suggested by some that we might repudiate 'the obligation. Fortunately that suggestion is not very seriously taken, nor made by anybody who is very serious.
But, Mr. Speaker, I would like parliament and the country to realize that however, manfully and fearlessly the government might have wrestled with this problem, it could not have done away with the railway debt which is Canada's debt, assumed by the people of Canada. The only possibility of relief from this burden lies in increased revenue from the railways and increased revenue from the railways can only come with increased tonnage and increased business. I think, Mr. Speaker, that not only in this country but in all countries men of good will are seeking for that specific which will bring back business and bring back tonnage not only to our own railways but to the railway and other transportation facilities of the different countries of the world.
We hear a great deal in this house about banking and currency. I am not of those who are skilled in the arts of the economist. I listen in reverential awe every time that an economist tells us that we can make ourselves rich by writing promissory notes, and that it is now possible to lift oneself by his boot straps. I have but very scant faith in shortcuts back to prosperity. In my view the way will be long, those who travel it must know industry, frugality, possibly penury. The government is providing an opportunity to examine the monetary, banking and currency

questions. The bankers and all interested will have an opportunity to suggest any and all specifics which may possibly yield a remedy. I contend it is not quite fair to say that the government has been entirely supine, that it has been negligent of the requirements of the country or deaf to the prayers of any section.
What about the trade agreements? Were they not conceived in the highest patriotism? Was the opportunity for their perfection not brought about by skilful, courageous and constant negotiations? Have those trade agreements not yielded a return, or have they not justified the hope for permanent betterment which was incident to their signing?

speechtext: No.

speechtext:
The hon. member says
no, and is entitled to his view. I think however he will agree at least that the majority in the house feel his decision has been taken a little too hastily. I for one believe that the faith, good will and spirit of sacrifice which characterized the signing of the agreements will not be entirely fruitless. I believe that the men who met in Ottawa, in an honest attempt to solve the difficulties of that portion of the world which they represent, came with a fund of information and experience, and an intent to deal fairly with all, which must bring good results.
There is one policy of the government which is bound to be of definite assistance: I refer to the back to the land movement. Many hon. members who have spoken concerning this movement have shown little faith. Only the other day the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) said, "You cannot expect to make a farmer out of an artisan who is out of a job." He went on to point out that probably the agricultural population had greater grounds for complaint than had any other element in Canada. I ask the house to consider, for a moment, the trend of events in Canada during the last fifty years. Fifty years ago only eighteen per cent of our population lived in cities and towns. Thirty years ago only thirty-seven per cent had gone to the larger centres of population. But the census taken only a year ago shows that 5,572,000 Canadians were urban dwellers, whereas only 4,800,000 were on the soil. How long can this progression from the soil towards the city continue? Is it not evident that of necessity there will result an unbalance and disequilibrium which, as in all cases of lack of equilibrium, is bound to manifest itself in an upset. Is it possible that we can take away

The Budget-Mr. Hackett
from the land a greater and greater number of people, and still maintain the strength and the poise characterized by perfect equilibrium. It is true that life on the land has not always been attractive, and that to-day the prices of farm products are extremely low. Yet, should we not recall that regardless of the fact that there is no money, regardless of the fact that there is a fair amount of drudgery, -and then some-the population on the land is the only population in Canada which is certain of food, shelter, clothing and fuel. True, there have been areas, such as that in Saskatchewan, which through an unusual occurrence were denied any returns from their fields. That condition was dealt with in an unusual way. I submit however it is true that on the land there is shelter from the economic storms which is not found in the cities and towns. I do not suggest that these men should return to the land to make fortunes by selling vast crops in the world's exchanges, or that they should return to enable the manipulators to make fortunes, but that their return should be for the purpose of supporting themselves and their families with the food they can get from the land. The plight in which hundreds of thousands of Canadians find themselves to-day, having to depend upon sources other than their own earnings for the food necessary to keep body and soul together is devastating. There comes from the very acceptance of that type of support a disintegration in the fibre of a people which is regrettable, and which is bound to manifest itself in a weakened spirit in this and future generations. I submit that back to the land is the most hopeful outlet from this dismal position in which we find ourselves at present. We are now at the spring of the year, and I ask the government to encourage the provincial and civic authorities to help the many thousands of people in the cities who were raised on the land to get back to the land. It is not necessary to take them away to remote regions; there are numerous opportunities in proximity to the large centres for a man to cultivate ten or twenty acres and provide himself and his children with the necessaries of life. I thoroughly believe that by disembarrassing the cities in this way, relieving them of the intolerable burden that now rests upon them, much can be done to overcome the present depression. We find in the United States cities like Chicago and Detroite-unfor-tunately we have them within our own area- which are on the verge of bankruptcy. Some have even failed to meet their obligations, because of the money they have been forced to spend to provide food for their citizens. It may mean a return to a more frugal mode
of life, but what of that? It may mean a lesser margin for luxury, but what of that, when starvation seems to be the alternative?
I submit, Mr. Speaker, it is impossible for this country to continue much longer the generosity-that may be an improper word-of the dole that has been meted out for the last three or four years. It is beyond our resources; the substance is not there for it.
One other matter about which I should like to say a few words is expenditure. Many people wince to-day under the burden of taxation. Others find in a disinclination to pay taxes what they take to be the growing pains of statesmanship. They say, why should the government levy $70,000,000 additional taxes? Why does not the government stop spending, retrench to the extent of $70,000,000?
I have pointed out the futility of that suggestion with regard to the railways, but one sees in the press news items and editorials which take the view that increased taxation is not necessary, that the budget could be balanced by reducing expenditure. I think it well that the people should have these facts placed clearly before them. This year we have estimated that the cost of government will be $445,000,000. Of that sum $369,000,000 represents ordinary expenditure. Every penny of that amount, less $143,000,000, is a fixed charge, something that cannot be escaped, something that is nailed down. We find among the items which constitute this total $138,000,000 of interest charges. There is a deficit on the Canadian National Railways of $55,000,000; pensions and soldiers' care, $58,000,000; subsidies to provinces, $15,000,000; old age pensions, $12,000,000; unemployment relief, $35,000,000. We find that of the $143,000,000 which is controllable nearly the entire amount represents services. In the abstract everybody wants expenditure reduced in order that taxation may be reduced, but everybody does not seem to be aware that nearly that entire amount is spent in wages paid to somebody, and that when it is reduced-and it is being reduced by $14,000,000-somebody gets less wages or loses his job; and when somebody loses his job he is another candidate for the dole. These services are possibly wise, possibly useful; at any rate we are wedded to them, we want them, we complain if they are taken from us. Looking over some of the possibilities of curtailment-my hon. friends opposite and even my friends on this side will see that I have been indiscriminate in the selection-I find for instance that the Receiver General has an office in every one of the nine provinces. In Montreal his office is in the offices of the City and District Savings
The Budget-Mr. Hackett

Bank, who perform the service for $25,000 a year and lose money on it. Is it necessary that there be an office in each of the maritime provinces? Of course not; there is more business done in three weeks in the Montreal office than there is in three years, I was going to say, in the maritime provinces-

speechtext: Order.
