speechtext:
But attempt to take away one of these offices, and you will be opposed with much vehemence by my hon. friends from the maritime provinces, on both sides of the house. And if one attempted the same thing in the prairie provinces the result would be similar. I merely take this as an example to show how difficult curtailment is, although it be necessary. Everyone knows that the estimates of the Department of Agriculture have suffered a considerable reduction: $2,792,000 have been taken from its estimates since 1930. We know7 that the department gives excellent service. Take the experimental farms; they are useful, well manned, economically run, but the question is, can we afford them? Yet try to close up one and find out what would be the attitude of the area it serves. The same is true in regard to forestry; both agriculture and forestry are essentially within the ambit of provincial activities, yet the federal government spends large sums of money in that work. If an, attempt were made to reduce those services I fear there would be much discontent.
Let us move to national defence. I dare say the number of units could be reduced without materially interfering with the efficiency of the service as a training or fighting agency, yet if either party attempted to curtail or restrict or do away with any of these units there would be much ado. Old age pensions and war pensions make heavy demands ipon us. We recall that a few years ago pensions were increased because of the increased cost of living. Now7 that the cost of living has fallen is it not possible to make a corresponding reduction in pensions? We all know that anything affecting the returned soldiers is an extremely difficult and delicate matter to deal with, yet I submit to that gallant body that someone must lead the way. Everyone wants reductions but no one wants to give up very much himself; he wants the reduction to be made at the expense of someone else. Bondholders are receiving 4| per cent, 5 per cent and 5i per cent to-day. They may not be anxious to take a lesser return, but it may be necessary for them to do so at an early date.
Much has been said about the tax on sugar.
It is unfortunate that a commodity so univers-(Mr. Hackett.]
ally used and so vitally necessary should be taxed, yet I think there are possibilities of good even in this tax. I would suggest to the government that they cause to be printed small tags indicating that this tax is to be used in aid of the Canadian National Railways, let us say; one of these tags might be attached to each package of sugar so that the individual buying the sugar would realize that the government is not a beneficent Santa Claus but that expenditures made by the government must be met by taxation.
I am one of those, Mr. Speaker, who believe that our government-and I say this without regard to party-has followed a protective, paternal, socialistic theory which seems to permeate the whole administrative fabric. Unless we are w'illing to turn sharply to the right we will find that our charges will continue to increase. Every politician knows before he is out of his nonage that it is impossible to cut sheer across either the history or the habits of a people and start afresh from a clean edge, but I submit that unless the people of Canada are willing to depart from the principles of socialism which they have introduced into their government by socializing their means of transportation, their means of communication, their production of power and to some extent their methods of buying and dealing in certain commodities; unless they are willing to do something to resurrect the rugged individualism of the past, we can only expect to follow the course of those nations that have yielded to this insidious doctrine and that to-day are under the control of dictators. If our people can be made to realize that services must be paid for, and that the people must pay for them, they may be willing to yield up in aid of economy a good many of the excellent services which are being lavished upon them at the present time, not because those services are not well administered, not because they do not add much to the ease of life, but because at the present time the Canadian people cannot afford them.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel it my duty to my constituents of the great county of Pontiac to give an account of my stewardship. First I should like to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) on the exceedingly able manner in which he presented his budget to this house on March 21. I am strongly in favour of that budget and of the policies of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), whose courage and ability have done much to see Canada through this time of crisis.

The Budget-Mr. Belec
The county of Pontiac, Mr. Speaker, is one of the largest counties in Quebec, if not in Canada. It is rich in minerals, water power, timber and agricultural products, and particularly in red blooded Canadianism. We have the sturdy sons and graceful daughters of those brave pioneers who did so much to build up our country. With such worthy, true citizens I believe we need have no fear for the future, because in the past few years we have overcome obstacles greater than ever confronted us before.
I have such a diversified county to represent, Mr. Speaker, that I must divide my speech into two parts; first I will deal with the mines and then I will have a word to say with regard to agriculture. First, however, I should like to say that in my opinion the coming year will see heavy orders for lumber placed in Canada by Great Britain. Russia has been supplying Great Britain's wants to our disadvantage, but I have reason to believe that this condition will not exist much longer. Already the agreements arrived at here in Ottawa are building up our trade, especially in agricultural products.
There are two matters of wide interest to my constituents which I should like to discuss at this stage of my remarks, and first I should like to refer to the highway between Sheen-boro and the Timiskaming district. I was in hopes that the provincial government would take advantage of the Dominion unemployment relief scheme to build up this highway. It would afford employment to a good many and open up a large forest and lake region, establishing communication between old Pontiac and Timiskaming. It would shorten the travelling distance between these two points by many miles and our people would not have to leave their own county to make the trip. Then in regard to the back to the land movement, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that I was amazed when I listened to the speech delivered by my hon. friend for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) with respect to the back to the land settlers. I have received many letters from settlers stating that they are well pleased with the treatment they received and are now receiving. In Riviere Solitaire, Lonely River, region over 400 families settled there since early last spring. They have a parish priest, a hospital with good equipment, and two post offices are to be established shortly. I visited that region, Mr. Speaker, long before there were any settlers, and I was amazed to see the large tract of land, thousands of acres, and if it were cleared it would make the best farming section in the province of Quebec.
I want to tell the house that I have the biggest county in Canada. I visited every corner of it last summer and I was glad to go to the mining section where there is no depression. Quebec's gold production-all in the county of Pontiac, amounted to 401,105 fine ounces last year. This was an increase of 34 per cent over 1931. The Noranda copper mine is the large producer, and the Siscoe, Granada and the O'Brien Cadillac all showed an improvement in output last year. In addition, considerable active prospecting was carried on, and at the Beattie property a large low-grade gold mine will commence production early in 1933; an 800-ton mill was completed, and low cost of operation is expected.
Last, year, as I have indicated, the production of gold in Pontiac county totalled 401,105 fine ounces valued at 88,291,576. In 1931, the gold produced amounted to 300,075 fine ounces valued at 86,203.101. So you see, Mr. Speaker, that our great Noranda and other mines are increasing their output and doing much to relieve unemployment and bring about better conditions. Our mines have shown the ability to survive the worldwide economic crisis and great credit is reflected upon the management and employees of the mines for their successful work. In total value of output mining is exceeded only by agriculture and forestry, but our mines in Pontiac, with their many requirements for all kinds of materials necessary to their successful operation, are playing an important part in the general industrial life in Canada.
In regard to agriculture, the different countries of the world, as well as the different classes of our business interests in Canada, to-day realize more than ever that the restoration of agricultural prosperity is the first and most essential national necessity. It has been said by many hon. members in this debate that agricultural soundness depends upon the more thorough development of the live stock industry as the basis. Our soils require and demand this change. The present government are true to their promise to encourage and foster the live stock industry. They have restored a better sire policy, have bonused better breeding stock so essential to improved grade, as well as lower cost of production. They also, upon assuming power, raised the duties on poultry, dairy and other live stock products. True, our prices have been low but we have no control of world prices; therefore when there is an exportable surplus of any product, the domestic price of such product is influenced by that price. On the other hand, of the products we can protect, the price has
The Budget-Mr. Belec

been maintained more nearly normal than in any other country under present conditions. For instance butter prices have been ait times 10 cents per pound better than in London, England, during recent months.
The Prime Minister has made great efforts since assuming power to secure our proper place in the British market, the greatest market in the world. The agricultural stabilization fund provided for in the present budget gives direct assistance to the farmers. It increases returns to the farmer by 12 per cent, placing the value of the English pound at $4.60 by direct payment from the treasury to make up for the difference between exchange value which is now $4.10. This, it is true, is on export products only, but the price of export surpluses naturally becomes home market prices. It will therefore increase the value of a 200 pound hog at the present exchange rate and market value by $1.50. It will therefore increase the farmer's returns on one load of 15 hogs more than an amount sufficient not only to pay his sugar tax, but to buy more sugar than the average family in Canada would use in twelve months.
This should also increase the price of poultry and agricultural products in view of the fact that considerable poultry has been at different seasons of the year exported to the United Kingdom. It will be recalled that last fall
1,000,000 pounds of poultry was exported to the British market bringing reasonably good returns to the producers. Had the agricultural stabilization plan been in effect at that time, it certainly would have increased the returns substantially. It should also prove to be of real value to those in the riding whom I have the honour to represent, who are interested in cheese manufacturing as we export a large amount of cheese annually and therefore it is one product that almost at all times is priced according to world conditions and overseas markets. It should raise the price of cheese at least one cent per pound or more, which after all is an important factor in view of the present dairy situation.
It is only by more milk being manufactured into cheese that the domestic butter prices can be improved. We hear a good deal with reference to the overproduction in milk producing districts even near the larger cities such as Toronto, Montreal and so forth. This oversupply invariably forces the price down to levels that are even below the cost of production. By the stabilization fund as presented by>
the government, our export market for cheese is bound to be improved, thereby consuming an increased volume of milk production.

It can readily be appreciated by at least everyone interested in the dairy business that it will have a stable influence on the domestic market. It will be noted that this fund is not applicable to butter exports, chiefly for the purpose of encouraging expansion of the cheese manufacturing business. It has been recognized for many years that Canada can make as fine cheese as is made in the world and has for forty years maintained an extensive foreign market for this production; while other countries with much more favourable climatic conditions can produce high grade butter more successfully and cheaper than we can in Canada. It would therefore appear that if Canada's exports of dairy products are to be increased it must be through an expansion in cheese manufacturing as well as such special products such as condensed milk and so forth. This must be done before any effort is made to develop our butter trade in other markets where that product meets with such strong competition. Every housewife in the rural districts of this country will realize that her returns in the dairy and poultry and products will be materially improved by this plan.
As a farmer I find myself in favour of the proposals made by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) for the appointment of a live stock export products commission to encourage more careful and uniform grading and to ensure if possible a greater regularity of supply to overseas markets. The United Kingdom buys a large amount of foodstuffs and Canada should make every possible effort to secure markets which we lost through the carelessness of the former government.
I also believe lowering of interest rates would help agriculture a great deal. The farmer to-day is carrying a heavy burden of debt incurred when prices were much higher and is carrying a debt on those values at a very heavy rate of interest as well. I believe he is sharing an undue burden at the present time and that an equalization of conditions is absolutely essential in order that he may restore, for the common interest of all, prosperity that must by necessity be born in agriculture first.
At six o clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I wish first of all to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) on the very able

way in which he presented the country's budget. Finance ministers during the present crisis have a very difficult task to perform, and whether or not we agree with the finance minister's budget proposals and his system of taxation, we must all admit that he presented the budget in an admirable manner.
This year, as during the last three years, we have unfortunately a very large deficit. I do not think any member of the house expected anything else. I do not think the government could have expected anything else; for in spite of the fact that the world is passing through a very difficult period the government I believe could not have done more to aggravate the situation than they have done in the last three years. We have only to look at the enormous increases in the tariff to see how they have helped to crush the trade of this country and what a tremendous factor they have been in reducing our revenue from customs tariffs. We have only to look at the exchange dumping duties which were imposed by this government to see at once how they interfere with the 'business of importers. Further, we see an enormous curtailment in bank credit. Although that may not be the direct responsibility of the government, so long as they shelter the banks in the program which the latter are carrying out, the government must bear a certain share of the responsibility. Or we might look at the tremendous curtailment which has been made in public works in the last three years. That in itself has meant a reduction in purchasing power and increased difficulty in carrying on business, which must have diminished taxpaying power. In the last three years we have had to face an enormous increase in taxation. We cannot tax a people on the one hand, cancel money out of existence when it is paid, and then expect trade to grow. So, taken all in all, I do not think the government could have done much more than they have done by their policies in the last three years to curtail the purchasing power of the people, and for these reasons, Mr. Speaker, it was not surprising to find that we have a considerable deficit. The solution of the government for this problem is heavier taxation, on the one hand, and curtailment of public works on the other. They also give advice which was perfectly right a hundred and fifty years ago in an age of scarcity, when the people were advised to work longer hours and consume less, in other words produce more and consume less. But this is an age of plenty.
We have been given figures in a tremendous amount of detail in the budget so far as cash received and cash spent is concerned,
The Budget-Mr. Spencer
also cash borrowed and cash lent, but it seems to me that, in some respects, the budget could have been fuller than it was. For instance, we have never yet had a budget which presented to us -the total amount of national production and the total consumption in Canada in a single year. Why should we not in our total assets show the following three items: total production, total appreciation, total imports; and against them the total consumption, total depreciation, and total exports. If we had those items set out in the budget we should find that Canada, instead of being a poor country as so many people think, is not only a very rich country but is getting richer every year. Canada's assets in round figures are supposed to be 30 billions of dollar's. If an individual uses a good deal less of his income than he receives in the year he thinks he is fairly well off, and that is exactly the position of Canada, because she produces a great deal more every year than sine actually consumes. Therefore in a commodity and service sense, if not in the arbitrary financial sense, we are getting richer every year.
The Finance minister in his budget indicated a favourable trade 'balance of about
870,000,000, and he seemed to be pleased about it. Personally I think that if we took all the trade figures into consideration we should regret very much the questionable showing. For instance, while the government boasts of having a favourable trade balance of 870,000,000 we have to admit, on the other hand, that our export trade 'has suffered a drop to the tune of $250,000,000. If we go on at 'that rate it will be quite possible eventually to have a favourable trade balance of $100,000,000 and yet do much less trade than we have done even in the past year.
There are certain things in the budget which I am very glad indeed to support, and I express my appreciation for their inclusion. First of all I want to congratulate the government upon deciding to appoint a royal commission to look into the whole banking and financial situation. Such an inquiry is long overdue, but even at this late date, if the commission is appointed and it is, in the words of the Finance minister, "an unbiased one and above-suspicion commission," there is no reason why it should not be productive of enormous good, particularly if it reports before the Bank Act comes up for revision next year. I sincerely hope that when the personnel of the commission is being chosen, great care will be taken to select men of worldwide repute, -and I trust that the scope of the commission will be as wide as is necessary.
The Budget-Mr. Spencer

I also want to congratulate the Minister of Finance upon his reference to the necessity of cutting down debit and interest rates. While it was all right for him to make that statement and to hope that an improvement might be brought about, it is within the government's power to bring about decided reductions in bath debt and interest charges. I also wish to congratulate the government upon the effort that is at last being made to help out the agricultural situation by setting up an agricultural stabilization fund. Although it is something in the nature of a bonus, and although bonuses may not be right in principle, at the same time when other industries are getting help from the government in this and other ways, it is only fair that agriculture should also be considered. My criticism is that consideration was not given to agriculture just about three years earlier.
It will also be very reassuring to importers to know that they are going to get some relief through the partial elimination of the adverse exchange dumping duties. To have carried on an import business in Canada during the last two or three years must have put any business man to a very severe test. I appreciate that the income tax rates have been made a great deal steeper than they were. If I had any criticism at all it would be that larger incomes should have been taxed even to a greater extent. I have under my hand figures given me a few months ago by the Income Tax department showing incomes in the fiscal years 1927-28 and 1930-31. In the earlier year only 8,510 people paid taxes on incomes ranging between $10,000 and $50,000; in 1930-31 there were 12,848 paid on those incomes. In 1927-28 only 345 people paid taxes on incomes between $50,000 and $100,000, whereas in 1930-31 there were 470. While only 75 people in the earlier year paid taxes on incomes of $100,000 and over, in the later year there were 131. So hon. members will note that in every instance those large incomes increased despite the bad business period through which we have been passing.
There are certain unpleasant factors in the budget which I should like to draw to the attention of the Minister of Finance. I regret very much the general trend of deflation in which the government is persisting. Up to the present time it has cost us dearly enough, and if it continues it will cost us a great deal more. Personally I can see the ultimate possibility of a financial crash if this policy is not changed. We cannot tax ourselves into prosperity, and apparently that is what we are

trying to do. I should like to place on Hansard certain figures taken from the last three budgets. In 1931 we had a deficit of $94,500,000. The reply of the government was to increase taxation in the following year to an equal amount. In the year 1932. instead of balancing the budget, unfortunately we were $119,000,000 short, and again somewhat similar efforts were made to balance the budget. In that year there was increased taxation, and in one way and another $50,000,000 was lopped off the estimates for public works, etc. However, such measures have not had the desired effect, and we find that this year we are faced with a deficit, including that of the Canadian National Railways, of about $156,000,000. Again I say we cannot tax ourselves into prosperity.
I am sorry to see the sales tax placed on certain commodities which were previously exempt. This will be a consumers' tax and will be paid very largely by those who, to use the common phrase, are the least able to bear it. I have no doubt the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has had voluminous correspondence regarding the tax on sugar. No doubt we all eat about the same amount of sugar, but some of us who may be in a better financial position may be able to afford it. There is no doubt it will hurt the poor householder, and particularly those in the country who can a considerable amount of wild fruit. The extra tax will make the canning more expensive.
The next item which I purpose to criticize I hope the government will see fit to change, namely that affecting soldiers' pensions. There may be a few ex-soldiers in the service who are receiving very large pensions and also a considerable allowance by way of a wage or salary. However, taking all in all, the proposed change would be a great hardship, and the amount of extra money collected would be infinitesimal as compared with the hardship involved. I am sorry, further, to see the tax on postal notes increased from one to three cents. No doubt this change will have the effect of driving business to the private banks. When we have an institution of our own such as the post office, in my view we should do everything possible to support it.
With regard to the criticism by the Minister of Finance concerning any suggestion of controlled inflation, I have a few comments to make. At the outset I shall quote from the Commercial Intelligence Journal of February 25, 1933, issued by the Department of Trade

The Budget-Mr. Spencer
and Commerce. At page 262 I find an article concerning Australia under the following head-note :
Improvement in Australian Financial Outlook, 1932
In part the article is as follows:
There are, however, some features apparent which distinctly point to the improvement, these including a return to stable government and a bountiful supply of cheap money. This latter has resulted in a readjustment of all capital values to a higher level, and the nominal increase in wealth and confidence is being reflected in a greater freedom of credit. The increasing confidence over the past few months has had a stimulating effect on public spending, and at the close of the year the sentiment was one of restrained optimism.
W ould that Canada could say the same thing! Unfortunately we are realizing that we are getting into a more critical position as the months go by. The government seems to have two pet obsessions, the one to balance the budget and the other to have a favourable trade balance. I should like to point out first that we could balance the budget, and continue to balance it, but at the cost of bringing the people to a very low standard of living; secondly, a favourable balance of trade means little if in the effort we lose trade valued at hundreds of millions of dollars.
The present situation in Canada is unique. A rich country, yet we are simply twiddling our thumbs, as it were, and not making use of our great natural advantages. I believe our inactivity lies in the fact that our problem is financial, and we have not tackled it from the proper angle. For instance, from Halifax to Vancouver we are badly in need of public works. At the same time there are in Canada about 800,000 unemployed, and we are continually adding to their ranks. Those men would be only too anxious to find employment on public works; instead they are kept on relief. Although we have plenty of food in the country we are feeding through public charities about 1,300,000 people. Again, our railway problem is caused not because people do not want to travel or send freight, but because they cannot afford to do either except to a very limited extent. We have the great industries of agriculture, forestry, fishing and manufacturing, with possibilities of tremendous production, yet all of them at the present time facing bankruptcy. We have much sickness in this country-in times of stress such as this there is always more than in normal times-yet many of our doctors and nurses have not enough to do, and many others are idle because people cannot pay. Never more
than at this time do we need life insurance, but during the period from 1930 to 1932 inclusive live insurance policies surrendered amounted to 8782,500,000, and insurance lapsed amounted to 81,224,000,000. These, Mr. Speaker, are serious figures. It only shows the extraordinary intensity of the financial crisis through which this country is passing, and which I think could be in large measure alleviated if the right thing were done. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) the other day informed the house that during the last few' years the gaol population of this country has doubled. These problems will not be solved by the cutting of wages and salaries; that is no final solution. The only benefit is that in some instances there is an equality of sacrifice where high salaries are reduced; otherwise in the aggregate it is a bad thing, because it is cutting down purchasing power, the one thing we need more than anything else.	*
The reasons for the lack of purchasing power, I take it, are largely two. First is inequality of income. That is being adjusted to a certain extent, by income and other taxation. Secondly the government does not seem to appreciate the fact that the total amount of money paid out in the cost of producing goods is never equal to the price of the goods. That being so it is necessary to put new money into circulation, and that new money should not be put into circulation through credits in the shape of debt, but by drawing on the national credit of the country, and that without interest. New money to-day is put into circulation only for productive purposes. As long as that is done we will always have difficulty in getting rid of our so-called surplus goods. We have to find a means of putting new money into operation through the consumers' channel.
There are certain facts it seems to me that we should face, and face boldly. First we should recognize that we need more money, more purchasing power. Does the minister not realize that to-day bank loans are over
8600,000.000 less than they were four years ago? Does he realize what that means to business? We in this corner have advocated controlled inflation. Those who would criticize us leave out the "control;" that is their fault, not ours. We stand solidly for controlled inflation. We recommend trying to get to a definite agreed-upon price level, and putting new money into circulation until we get to that price level; we should then have controlled inflation.
The Budget-Mr. Spencer

We must find a means of getting the food to the people without its going through the channels of charity as it is doing to-day.
We have to find the means of putting people to work. Surely that is not beyond man's power and initiative; when there is so much to be done in every part of this country, surely it is not beyond our power to find ways and means of putting men to work.
Another problem we have to face, and I am glad to see it is mentioned in the budget speech, is the debt problem, whether private, municipal, provincial or federal. We cannot go on with a dear dollar and cheap goods and expect to meet these liabilities.
We have to recognize that we should show the same consideration to commodity wealth as we show to financial wealth. For instance, there is no reason why money put into a business that is for the benefit of the community should not be just as sacred as money put out at loan. The government Should alter its policy with regard to public works and taxes. It seems to me it is a wrong process to tax heavily when times are bad; taxation should be heavy when times are good and people have the money to pay. On the other hand public works should not be encouraged when times are good, when business is active, but should be carried on a large scale when times are bad and business generally is frozen. To-day general business is too nervous to start the wheels of progress moving; the government is the only body in a position to start the machinery, and if that were done' there is no doubt that general commerce would follow.
I would like to quote from Mr. V. C. Vickers who wrote a preface to Doctor Eisler's book, Stable Money. I may say that Mr. Vickers was a director of the Bank of England from 1910 to 1919. He said in part:
If for the time being we concentrated a little more upon assisting productive work, and a little less upon balancing the budget, it would, in the end, be better for us all. Our aim should be to go forward to a new economy, not back to the old regime.
I particularly commend that statement to the finance minister.
In closing I should like particularly to draw the government's attention to the following quotation, and to suggest that consideration of the principle stated therein is long over due:
A new orientation of national policy is needed to take care of the interests of the consumer, but there is no sign of it, nor likelihood of it, so long as the general belief is that prosperity at home is dependent upon exporting to markets abroad.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are
a few .observations which I should like to make upon the budget. The previous speaker (Mr. Spencer) like others from the same side, has complained about the new taxes. It was not expected, sir, that the budget brought down by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) would be a pleasing or cheery document. At no time in the history of Canada has a government been faced with problems more gigantic, problems of greater difficulty. Governments the world over are grappling with tremendous financial difficulties, and all that could be expected was that the government would introduce drastic measures to meet the situation.
A cheering feature of the budget is the agricultural stabilization fund. From it there will be paid to exporters to the British market the difference between the price actually received for the pound sterling and $4.60. In other words, if the pound sterling falls below $4.60, as it is at present, the difference will be made up from the fund. This feature of the budget should be heartily commended; it will bring a higher price for the products the farmer exports, it will encourage production and will result in bringing wealth from outside to the agricultural districts in Canada. This in turn will stimulate trade and work to the good of all.
Last fall I was criticized by one hon. member for having made a promise during the by-election to the effect that a premium would be granted on cheese. The advantages which will result from the stabilization fund, in connection with milk products, doubtless are more than equivalent to those that would result from the granting of a premium, and I am sure the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) will not contradict me when I say that I repeatedly made pressing representations to him to have cheese included under that fund. This stabilization plan is more than a bonus on agricultural products exported to Great Britain; it is an attempt at equalization. During this depression agriculture has taken the hardest blow; farm products have shown the greatest shrinkage in value, and the farm income has been greatly reduced though the articles that must be purchased have been kept at high prices. This measure introduces some attempt at equalization, and I am sure there will be no complaints so long as all classes contribute equally during hard times and share equally in times of prosperity.
I sincerely regret the necessity of taking up the time of the house with personal matters, but I think it better that these points should be settled once and for all. Some hon. mem-

The Budget-Mr. Bourgeois
bers who have not forgotten the defeat of their candidate in the Three Rivers-St. Maurice by-election have expressed certain innuendos with regard to promises made by the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) concerning the expenditure of some $700,000 on the Three Rivers wharf and $50,000 for a retaining wall along the river in the bay of Shawinigan and St. Boniface parishes; they say these promises have not been fulfilled. On October 25 the hon. member for St. Johns-Iberville (Mr. Rheaume) informed this house that it was his intention to ask some question in this connection. I expected that the hon. member would formulate his questions and have them included in the orders of the day, but so far as I know he has not done so as yet. For his information and for the information of his friends let me say that the sum of $700,000 has been spent by the government in the construction of a wharf at Three Rivers, and that the retaining wall which the inhabitants of the Bay of Shawinigan and St. Boniface parishes and the northern part of St. Maurice county have been requesting for the past twenty-two years is now an accomplished fact. While the main principle of the government's policy is the curtailing of expenses I dare, for it is my duty, to request the building of sheds on the new wharf.
From the Montreal press I understand that the government, by granting the land required, intends to assist in the construction of an additional elevator at Sorel. I do not wish to object to that proposition, but I would suggest that the elevator be erected at Three Rivers, because lake St. Peter constitutes an obstacle to navigation at Sorel. From early in December until late in April the Sorel harbour is blocked by the ice from lake St. Peter, so the harbour of Three Rivers has the advantage of having navigation open two months longer than is the case at Sorel. Three Rivers is a first class shipping port and is the centre for a considerable portion of the cattle shipping trade on the St. Lawrence river. I sincerely regret that the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) is not in his seat, because I know he is an authority in this matter. I invite him to pay us a visit and look over our facilities. I am sure that he would corroborate my opinion. Our position, near lake St. Peter on the north shore of the St. Lawrence river and at the mouth of the St. Maurice, gives us the advantage of the natural deep water of the St. Lawrence while we also command the vast St. Maurice territory, which exceeds 17,000 square miles in area. Until a few years ago the city was forced to struggle
along with the development of its own harbour, but later this work was taken over by the federal government. Since that was done rapid progress has been made in the construction of a great permanent harbour, and at present Three Rivers boasts of the facilities it can offer all classes of inland and ocean going ships. An additional 3,600 feet of wharves has been completed and will be ready for use with the opening of navigation, and with the completion of the present building program Three Rivers will have a modern commodious harbour. Any person visiting Three Rivers will be convinced that we have the most advantageous spot for the purposes of the cattle shipping trade. From the city limits, extending westward along the St. Lawrence river for several miles, we have a magnificent tract of beautiful grazing land, as level as a prairie, and watered by several streams. This land is traversed by the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, with a branch line to deep water on the wharves, forming without exception the most desirable storage for cattle trade which can be possibly imagined.
I must not omit a reference to the supplies required for feeding cattle on the Atlantic voyage. At Three Rivers any required quantity of first class hay and oats can be purchased and at lower price than at other ports of the St. Lawrence. A certain quantity of live stock can also be purchased for shipment, in Three Rivers, and in the back country, which includes Shawinigan Falls and Grand'Mere; so that, in fact, all circumstances combine to facilitate in a remarkable degree this most important branch of the Canadian export trade at the port of Three Rivers.
I may add that several petitions have been circulated and signed throughout the Three Rivers district requesting that a measure should be adopted by the federal government in order that 'the Canadian National railway should reach Three Rivers at a point situated between Charette Mills or another point on the Canadian National railway. I submit that if, owing to the conditions now prevailing, this cannot be done, it would be possible to utilize the Canadian Pacific line from Les Piles. The only thing which would have to be done would be for the federal government to compel the Canadian Pacific Railway to allow the Canadian National Railways to use its line from Gameau to Three Rivers. It is to be noted that under section 16 of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act as passed by the Senate on the 23rd of February

The Budget-Mr. Bourgeois
of this year, 1933, and now under consideration in the house, this scheme should be absolutely realizable.
In regard to the measures adopted by this government in connection with unemployment and farm relief, it may be said that on the whole, and taking into account the urgency of the situation, they were beneficial. But, without caking any blame on those who were charged with the distribution of the money voted by this parliament for relief purposes, one may ask whether with the experience acquired since that relief policy has begun, some modification should not be made to it. We are all agreed on the principle that people should go back to the land, provided there is a reasonable hope of their earning a living. But the first thing to ascertain would undoubtedly be: Have they the natural disposition and the experience required to earn their living in that way? Then consideration should be given to the place where these would-be farmers are sent. They should not, as it has been said, have to find their way through stumps and underbrush. In many parts of Canada, at least in the province of Quebec, there are farms, small farms which have been already under cultivation and which have for one reason or another, been abandoned, their owners having migrated to industrial centres in Canada or to the United States.
Without agreeing with my hon. friend from Temiscouaita (Mr. Pouliot) concerning the administration of the back to the land movement, as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, my suggestion would be that the money which the government intends to contribute in helping the unemployed should, first and principally, be used in attempting to place them on those farms where they would have far greater chances of making a living than by becoming settlers on undeveloped lands in remote regions.
While disclaiming any desire to be an alarmist, the hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) has lately told this house that communistic activities are more acute and dangerous in this country than in many years past. The agents of Russia are busy fomenting troubles among the unemployed and the economically distressed. Reds are putting forth renewed efforts to undermine the loyalty of veterans' associations, it is said in Mail and Empire, April 4, 1933, by the familiar method of penetration from without. The returned men are invited to attack the authorities. The Minister of Justice is no doubt in possession of specific information from the veterans' association that overt acts are contemplated 
in certain populous centres. It is no doubt for such reasons that he asked for the means to increase the strength of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in the event of possible emergency. The minister and the government will undoubtedly have the backing of every loyal person in adopting a policy of adequate preparedness. These are days of stress and strain, when the decent citizen looks to the powers that be for timely, efficient and effective protection. It is to be noted that at President Roosevelt's request the United States congress is putting through severe legislation to prevent any disloyal section of the United States press publishing information inimical to the national welfare. One may doubt whether section 98 of our criminal code is sufficient to repress seditious activities which, it is reasonable to surmise, are caused by communistic propaganda. It is known that there is among us a campaign conducted by communists who are not only advocating and diffusing ideas subversive of our economic ant' political institutions, but attacking religious ideals in general and overtly preaching atheism Their insults to Christianity and their blasphemies against God are so violent and so frequent that every Christian in this country must believe it is time such offences were repressed and punished by our criminal law and I submit that our criminal code should be amended accordingly.
In Montreal there are two so-called labour
universities, one on Craig street and the other on Montcalm street. At those places meetings are held every night attended by numerous unemployed workmen who are taught the pernicious doctrines of soviet Russia. In consequence attempts to burn, and actual burnings of churches in the province of Quebec have reached a point where surely the authorities would feel it necessary to take drastic action to discover what is beyond those dastardly acts. The utmost condemnation of such acts must be felt by all; indeed it is difficult to imagine any one capable of such conduct who is not out of his mind. It is well known that the psychology of the Russian five year plan, which was put into effect on October 21, 1928. is one of militant communism and militant atheism or aniti-religious propaganda.
The man's the gowd for a' that.
The refrain of Burns' immortal song is just the reverse of that theory. "There is a divine law of rewards. When the Creator gave us the earth with its fruitful soil," said William Jennings Bryan, " The sunshine with its warmth and the rains with their moisture," he proclaimed as clearly as if his voice had

The Budget-Mr. Bourgeois
thundered from the clouds:	Go, work, and
according to your industry and your intelligence, so shall be your reward." . Let us hope that our country, "this blessed country, this earth, this realm, this Canada," shall ever escape the danger of being ruled according to socialistic principles.
It is through immigration that the socialistic and communistic ideas may subvert our economic system. It was then wisely that on August 7, 1930, when he had been carried to power on the twenty-eighth of the preceding month the right hon. the Prime Minister caused an order in council to be adopted putting an immediate stop to immigration, and now every immigrant in order to be allowed to come and settle in this country is bound to go through the strictest immigration formalities. I dare say that on account of the splendid services he has rendered to this our country, the Prime Minister, like the celebrated English statesman, the Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, may rightly say:
I have faith in our race and in our nation.
I believe that all the forces and enthusiasm of which democracy alone is capable will complete and maintain that splendid edifice upon greatness, which, commenced under aristocratic auspices, has received in those later times its greatest extension, and that the fixity of purpose and strength of will which are necessary to this end will be supplied by that national patriotism which sustained the most strenuous efforts and made possible the greatest sacrifice.
In my opinion the Prime Minister is and will remain among us as a teacher of the will to do and a professor of energy. He should be valued not in the abstract, but with due regard to the conditions of the time. I have not in the least the desire to minimize the worth of any of our statesmen of by-gone years. A thorough Canadian should admire in their turn all those who have given to this country more comfort, more renown or glory. The Prime Minister has a very high conception of the functions of his office, and he fulfils them with a rare firmness. He has adopted a program and stuck to it in the extremely difficult circumstances which have existed since he has been the head of this government. All of us, barring all differences of opinion and party feelings, should honour him as a servant of our country who is doing his duty manfully at a time when the interest of Canada requires, of course, that every Canadian shall do his duty, but especially he who has in his hands the direction of our destinies.
The comments I have just made, Mr. Speaker, in connection with the budget and the criticisms I have ventured to develop with regard to socialism and communism may have been lengthy and somewhat tedious, but I
trust I shall be forgiven. Now, may I invite you, sir, and all the hon. members of the house to come to Three Rivers, the second oldest city of Canada, to participate in the festivities which will take place in July 1934, in commemoration of the third centenary of its foundation. While the city of Three Rivers has been and is still affected by the economic depression, perhaps in a larger measure than most other industrial centres; while its main industry, the pulp industry, lies in a state of quasistagnation and leaves a large number of men and women without employment, the citizens of Three Rivers, in a worthy spirit of optimism and because they have faith in the future, have come to the conclusion that, in spite of the difficulties and anxieties of the times, they should, as a matter of duty, celebrate this anniversary.
Our city, founded by Sieur de la Violette, has a history which reads both like a poem of heroism and an adventurous tale. For a hundred years Three Rivers was a most important post for the fur traders. It was also there that was created and developed, so to speak, that type of man so truly Canadian, the shantyman, who lived in the wide open spaces; who heard the tumultuous voices of the falls and impetuous torrents; who loved to seek the adventures and brave the dangers of lands beyond, and who filled the forest with the echoes of his songs. One may recall among the travellers or voyageurs from Three Rivers, such famous names as those of Nicolet, Godefroy, Chouart, of Hudson ibay fame, and Gaultier de Varennes, Sieur de la Yerendrye, of Rocky mountain fame, a great Canadian discoverer, and other names glorious and immortal in the annals of Canada.
It might also be recalled that Three Rivers was the cradle of metallurgy in Canada. For nearly a century and a half what is still known as Forges St. Maurice furnished the country with the iron products that it required. Of the three cities established on the shores of the St. Lawrence during the French regime, Three Rivers is decidedly not the most important, but while Quebec is the seat of the provincial legislature and Montreal the commercial metropolis, Three Rivers has doubtless charms of its own in which to glory on occasion.
To be particularly proud of such a city as Three Rivers, I am sure is permissible to one who was born there and who has the honour to represent that city in this parliament. This feeling on my part shall not, I am sure, astonish any of the members of this house who at the time of the Imperial conference in August, 1932, paid a visit to Three Rivers and observed its marvellous possibilities of development.
The Budget-Mr. Barrette

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the courage displayed by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), in bringing down a budget so burdened with taxation, is certainly worthy of praise. 1 especially wish to draw the attention of the house to the well established fact that alone the economic depression of which Canada, as well as the rest of the world, Buffers, has forced the government to resort to such a budget.
All members of this house realize, better than I can express it, the moral courage displayed by a government, when it risks its popularity by increasing the taxes which burden a nation. It is the outward and fearless expression of a government conscious of its duty. It is the accomplishment of this disagreeable duty which all statesmen have to face when the nation's credit, upon which the prosperity of the people depends, demands it.
Above all, the duty of our governments is to safeguard the nation's economic system, so rudely shaken by a world-wide depression and which the hon. member for Winnipeg North 'Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) would completely cast aside because as he states " the present economic system is responsible for the fact that a large number of people are out of work, and that both our natural resources and the social organization in this country serve the interests of a few and not those of the people, as a whole."
These two statements are baseless and the hon. member carefully avoided substantiating them. In what way is our present economic system responsible for the unemployment of so large a number of people? The hon. member does not state. This economic depression is world-wide, as the hon. member pointed out. Almost all countries differ in their economic systems and even Russia's economic regime was powerless against this depression. Ever since the world was created, at various periods, there have been economic crises in all countries and under all economic regimes. All forms of government were tried and none of them were able to stem the rising tide of economic crises.
This economic depression has been attributed to a thousand causes, however, there are plausible reasons to believe that the main cause is the lack of trust among nations as well as among individuals. It belongs to a moral order rather than to a material one. The world's wealth lias remained intact but badly distributed, and a large portion of it has remained unproductive owing to this lack of trust. It is clearly a trial sent by Heaven. The world was likewise upset when the erection of the tower of Babel was undertaken. 
The entire population of the world worked on the construction of this tower. It was the golden period of those past ages. All had work and cherished great hopes in the achievement of this gigantic tower which eventually would reach Heaven. Suddenly, God's hand smites the world. The workmen can no more understand one another as God has given them different languages. No more cooperation can exist. All their hopes have vanished. The tower remains unfinished, the people are left without work and they are forced to rest. That was, perhaps, the first world-wide economic depression. It must have been terrible since history has recorded the fact. It was certainly not the economic system of that period which was responsible for that crisis. It was a punishment inflicted upon human pride. Why not attribute the present crisis to the same cause?
Then, why assert that our natural resources and the social organization of the country's production are diverted to benefit a few? It is certainly an unfair statement. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) is fully aware that, if the working classes have no wrork, it is because those who had wealth have lost it and cannot carry on their industries. It is true that there are a few capitalists left and it is fortunate for us, and our few industries which remain. As long as there is a scarcity of wealthy people, we shall be deprived of industries and our people will be unemployed. Captains of industries are needed so that the people's savings may 'be invested and bear fruit. That is the work of financiers. The profits they make are infinitely small compared to the benefit the nation derives. During the periods of prosperity our working classes earned wages varying between $4 and $10 per day. Do you not think, sir, that our workmen would not gladly seethe fortunes lost by our financiers returned to them, so that they might again receive the wages they once earned and enjoy the prosperous days of the past.
Among all these wealthy men, there were certainly robbers and profiteers, but, even while robbing they contributed to the happiness of the people.
That the state should better control industrial trusts, I agree; but I do think it absurd to suppress them. The economic conquest is carried out just like a war is waged: with soldiers and generals. The soldiers are the workmen and the capitalists are the generals. The worker is therefore interested that his employer should make sufficient profits which will allow him to continue his operations, and, in fact, a good worker, is always glad to see his employer acquire wealth 'because he is

The Budget-Mr. Barrette
bound sooner or later to derive some benefit from it. Self-interest is one of the most potent incentives of life, it compels man to work and leads to achievement. It is the prime mover of human effort; it is the main incentive of production, trade, researches, discoveries, inventions and all human activities. All social organizations must tend to foster private initiative for the greatest welfare of the community and all political reforms tending to curtail the freedom of private individuals are directly opposed to human nature, destined to failure and lead to disorder. Human activities small and great, must be the result of private initiative to be beneficial.
If the lot of our people is to be improved, there is but one thing to do:	preach by
example and word the social and religious truths which alone can assure the progress and happiness of humanity. Preachers of religion should avoid persecuting, under the pretence of religion, their fellow-citizens; similarly those who are intent on reforming morals or society should avoid upsetting social institutions under pretence of social welfare and putting everything to the sword and fire. Let us point out to the people not only their rights but also their duties. Let us seek the means of being useful to others while serving our own interests. Let us seek the real aim of life. Let us remember that freedom is indispensable to attain moral progress, which, to be efficacious, must not be interfered with.
Mr. IRV'IXE: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I would draw your attention to the fact that there is not a quorum in the house.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. Barrette

have but two. Since 1927, the Auditor General's report shows that we have received $17,000,000 less for public works than to what we are entitled.
More than $4,000,000,000 have been expended on railways while our share has been only $489,000,000, that is $600,000,000 less than our quota. All our ports are neglected. The Montreal harbour owes its development to its citizens. We are entitled to double the number of grain elevators and many more wharves. And to mention more recent events, how can one justify the discontinuance of a certain undertaking in connection with the Canadian National Railways, at Montreal, which has left an open and large excavation in the centre of the metropolis, thus depriving the Canadian National Railways of an economic terminus, when millions of dollars are expended to complete the doubtful enterprise at Fort Churchill. The St. Lawrence channel should have been dredged to a depth of 35 feet, on a width of 600 feet, at least 10 years ago.
I never neglect an opportunity of reminding the Prime Minister and his colleagues of these grievances. That is the only source of our quarrels. However, I note that the Prime Minister greatly sympathizes with me and I still have hope of convincing him to take this question of French Canada out of Canadian politics by granting us the fair quota to which we are entitled in the administration of this country, especially, as I expect that the next house will be composed of 60 French Canadian members from Quebec, elected to uphold the principles and ideas advocated by the Conservative party, which are the best and wisest for the government of our country, but, especially, in order to insist that our rights be entirely recognized. The new imposts may not be popular; the hon. members of the opposition may be piously listened to by the people in distress; the gloomy description of our situation may still further dishearten our citizens; utterances like those of the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) may rouse the passions of the people; however, all these appeals to prejudice and human selfishness can in no way belittle the deep gratitude which our people feel toward the right hon. Prime Minister and his colleagues. A moral force emanates from their courageous attitude in facing the problems which rise daily and which they are busy in solving for the greatest welfare of our people.
Thus, further revenue had to be raised to consolidate our credit, assist those in want 
and help our people through this crisis; therefore, the government levies an impost on sugar, increases the income tax and taxes other articles.
With their good common sense the people fully understand that the moment taxes are levied, the rate payer's must be assessed. Bear in mind that the working or farming class does not form a caste apart and that it is as disagreeable to them to note that the village employer, merchant or banker is taxed; in either case, the workman or farmer knows that he will equally share in the distress or prosperity of his fellow citizens, whatever high position they may occupy. The people are fully aware that the present distress started higher up, by 'the financial losses made by the upper classes. The prosperity of a nation is closely linked to eveiy form of taxation, no matter how unequally distributed it may seem at first, it ends by reaching directly or indirectly all individuals.
All the government must decide is the amount necessary to administer the country's affairs. Should $300,000,000 be required, there will necessarily be $300,000,000 levied in taxes. If the government were in 'a position to know exactly .the salary or income of each individual, the problem of taxation would soon be solved, as all would be assessed in proportion to his resources. But, unfortunately, it is practically impossible to arrive at exact figures concerning the income of each individual. The government is therefore forced to resort to taxes easily collected which will bring in the revenue foreseen. The sugar tax will thus enrich the treasury by $20,000000. This anticipated amount is not gainsaid. We could analyse all taxes and always arrive at the same conclusion. We should avoid levying them, but, unfortunately, they are necessary. All we can request from the government is that it should only levy the taxes which really benefit the treasury.
I trust the hon. Minister of Finance will permit me to make a suggestion. Why not confine ourselves to customs duties and excise taxes, reducing the latter by 50 per cent, so as to foster domestic trade, and why not abolish all other imposts, such as taxes on corporations, sugar and sales tax, briefly, all existing taxes, and replace them by a 1 per cent tax on all bank transactions? The latter amounted to the enormous sum of $31,000,000,000 in 1931, and would have brought a revenue of $315,000,000 to the state. The collection of such a tax would not cost a cent to the government.

The Budget-Mr. Barrette
All banks would retain on. cheques presented at the teller's wicket, 1 per cent of the cheque amount, as a government tax. The majority of cheques are generally drawn to pay bills or debts, and the tax would fall on the payee, which after all would only amount to 1 per cent deducted on his bill. Thus, the poor man who has no banking account would be exempt from taxation, while those who have large banking accounts would be taxed according to their standing in the financial world. It would be a far more equitable tax than the income tax, because nobody could escape it. A 1 per cent surtax could be demanded for each endorser, other than the beneficiary, so as to avoid that the same cheque be used by various holders, thus avoiding the tax.
Note that with this proposed system, the 1 per cent tax is levied on the payee and not on the person who issues the cheque; there would be no inducement to pay with cash; and t'he banks, thereby, would have no fear of receiving less deposits.
Another advantage attached to this form of taxation would be that large companies as well as prominent financiers would be obliged to practically pay their taxes daily, thus their financial affairs would be better balanced than with the present system, which consists in paying at the end of the fiscal year an income tax, when, in the ordinary course of business, they have already invested their money in various enterprises and find it most difficult to raise the necessary cash to pay the enormous tax which the state collects each year, at a fixed period. And it is the moire burdensome because no person can figure out the amount he must pay before first making a complete survey of bis affairs; it is then too late to think of suppressing other expenses or industrial investments to meet this tax.
The uncertainty as to what the income tax will amount, necessarily makes capitalists very cautious and forces them to set aside, each year, much larger amounts than the tax calls for, because of the fear of making an error in their calculations; this actually deprives industry of a much larger amount than the tax collected.
The objections to the taxation which I suggest must necessarily be numerous, because all taxes meet with opposition. However, I wish to point out that this tax has a great redeeming quality; it will be economical and easy to collect. I believe that the cost of collecting the income tax and other excise 53719-246|
taxes, etc., amounts to more than $8,000,000 per year; while this 1 per cent impost would practically cost nothing to collect; because the channel through which the government gets its information already exists; the banks, at present, supply the government with monthly statements on cheques passing through their institutions. The government, therefore, has always this information on hand. The amount varies between $2,000,000,000 and $3,000,000,000 per month; thus banks when forwarding their monthly statements would simply have to inclose a cheque of 1 per cent on the amount mentioned in the statement. The government would, therefore, receive, monthly, a cheque varying between $20,000,000 and $30,000,000. I do not think that any doubt could foe cast on the honesty of our banking institutions as regards their statements; at all events, it would be an easy matter for a few government inspectors to check up the books of the various banks.
This tax is so simple in its practical application and so devoid of complication, compared to the existing tax system, that the government should have no hesitation in adopting it. What would be more simple than the collection of this tax; when a cheque is presented at the bank, the teller would only pay 90 per cent of the amount mentioned, and would debit the account of the client 100 per cent. At the end of each day, banks add the total amounts of cheques presented and debit their clients' accounts with said amounts. This operation would immediately indicate what amount is due to the government, namely 1 per cent of the total amount of the cheques. At the end of each month, banks would forward to the government a statement showing the total amount of the cheques debited to the accounts of their clients; this is actually in practice, it would therefore require no further outlay by the banks. In preparing their statement the banks would simply mention that they have deposited to the government's account 1 per cent of the total amount of cheques cashed. Is there any simpler system as regards tax collection? Compare this system with that of the present collection of the income tax, consider all the irregularities to which the latter system gives rise and the necessity the government is under of continuously checking up their employees and seeing that they carry out their duties, notwithstanding the always growing temptation of granting favours to their friends. There could be no possible favour granted to friends
3S94
The Budget-Mr. Barrette

with this 1 per cent tax, so that you suppress the factor of human weakness which should not be put to a test. All are aware of the corrupt practices of which the putting into force of the Volstead Act was the occasion in the United States; the Income Tax Act is similar to the Volstead Act and is destined sooner or later to corrupt officials and weaken the moral force of the whole administration. We should make a strong effort to abrogate all laws which are generally disregarded by the large majority of citizens. If by the [DOT]excessive severity of our laws, we tempt the great majority of our people to disregard them, we thereby tempt these same people to break other laws which are of a much higher moral order, the observance of which is absolutely necessary for the moral uplift of our people.
To foster agriculture I would suggest that the government erect cold storage plants, costing about $10,000 each in all farming counties. Farmers could then store their perishable products and banks could be authorized to loan to farmers 50 per cent of the par value of these products. In order to market these products abroad, I would suggest that the government promote a commercial organization of salesmen something similar to the organization existing in the past to induce immigrants to settle here. When we were endeavouring to increase the population of this country, we had immigration agents in all European centres liable to : send us immigrants. These agents were paid :a salary and a commission of so much per 'head. We thus succeeded in drawing thousands of immigrants to these shores, although such a policy cost us many millions of dollars.
I would suggest that the government appoint agents in all large European cities in a position to purchase our farm products. These agents would be supplied with a list of all our farm products in cold storage. In each respective country they could employ people who would visit the various retail stores offering for sale our farm products. Each day, orders thus obtained would be grouped to make up a complete cargo so that reasonable shipping rates could be had. In this way we would have abroad thousands of [DOT]clients, instead of being at the mercy of a few wholesale houses. It might be necessary to erect some cold storage plants in a few large European cities so as to always have on hand a surplus of our products for quick sales. The government could be reimbursed for this outlay by adding a small storage charge on the sale of these products.
JMr. Barrette.]
Is it not time, in order to further assist the Canadian farmer, that we should, as a measure of expediency, settle what is to be the minimum prices on farm products? For instance, why not decree that. the minimum price of butter should be 25 cents per pound and that of cheese 10 cents a pound. Such measures would tend to encourage the Canadian farmer to raise his spirit depressed by this crisis which has already lasted too long.
Other means of indirectly assisting the farming class and stemming unemployment would be to allow Canadian distillers to export alcohol, which would result in reopening again the doors of distilleries. WTe must bear in mind that a distillery of Melchers Gin standard, operated within the limits of my constituency, uses millions of bushels of Canadian grain, without mentioning the hand labour and by-products of these manufactures utilized by the farming class. Moreover, when the debate on the Robinson bill took place, it was proved, without a doubt, that alcohol exports brought into the treasury an amount varying between $15,000,000 and $20,000,000. Would not this amount have been sufficient to permit our government to carry on without levying a 2-cent tax on sugar? Such a measure would be well received by the people, because those who are making millions of dollars, to the detriment of our industries, have a questionable reputation, and to-day the United States doors are wide open to clandestine trade.
Other means of checking unemployment would be to further develop the Beauharnois power and St. Lawrence waterways. These two undertakings would give work to about forty or fifty thousand men and would completely relieve unemployment in this country. No doubt, sir, you are aware that between 1872 and 1878 there was a similar crisis in this country and that the construction of the Lachine canal contributed in a large measure to end that crisis.
Recently I received a letter from a Montreal friend who pointed out the necessity of curbing the electricity trust in Canada. The letter is as follows:
1280 Bernard Ave., Outremont,
March 28, 1933.
Mr. J. A. Barrette, M.P.,
Ottawa, Out.
Dear Sir,-
Pursuant to our conversation, I respectfully submit the following facts:
The Beauharnois Company such as organized, with its advantageous and permanent current contracts, provides for the payment of all interests on mortgages and bonds, and more-

over raises the value of the common stock to many millions of dollars, why then should not the original bondholders receive for their investment 100 cents on the $1?

Heat and Power Company sustained in their investments.
We feel confident that the leader of the government will not force the original bondholders to make such a gift to Mr. Holt and his silent associates, why not preferably make this gift to the people of Canada, if one absolutely wishes to be philanthropic.
With the slightest effort, the least gifted can calculate what the realizable profits the Beauharnois Company will make:

Now that all the risks entailed by the project are things of the past, a shameful proposal is suggested to those who risked their hard earned money under the pretence that alone the Montreal Light. It is a cunning scheme; they wish to acquire, by every possible means at their disposal, a sound and splendid enterprise to cover the poor investments made by Mr. Holt.
If the Beauharnois project passes into the hands of the ogre, it will no more be the imposing and gigantic undertaking which was the pride ol its promoters and of all the citizens of this province. At present in the United States, commissions are being appointed to inquire into the financial operations of the banker Pierpont J. Morgan. The Canadian people would very

much like to get to the bottom of the financial operations of Sir Herbert Holt; perhaps, they might find out how the people were exploited and robbed and whether it is possible to make these large financiers stump up what they have robbed from the public.
You are no doubt aware, sir, that the Quebec government has just enacted a measure permitting the exportation of electricity. Could not the Dominion government disallow such an act, so as to conserve all our electrical energy to develop our own industries? It behooves the Prime Minister, who has the exceptional advantage of being supported by a large and united majority, who repose in him their trust, beside having a great admiration for his achievements, it behooves,
I state, the Prime Minister to oppose such a measure. Will he follow the example of Mussolini, Hitler and Roosevelt who took advantage of their prestige to introduce in their respective countries new principles of government, setting aside class prejudices, financial influences and red tape procedure, which are inherent to all governments, in order to give their respective countries an administration rendered necessary by the present crisis, and which seems destined to solve, happily, their national problems.
